Bias cautions: This prompt was authored by an AI agent that may have an
opinion on the answer. Its framing may inadvertently constrain you to in-scope
refinements when the right answer is to question the scope. The work being
reviewed may be presented as further along than it should be. Before answering as
posed, briefly check whether this is the right question. If a different question
would be more useful, answer that one too.

## The decision

A tutorial teaches a team of ~3 developers to build a three-module .NET service
pipeline (`converter`, `persistence`, `watcher`) that talk over HTTP.

**The team model (settled by the operator, not up for debate):** ONE shared git
repository. EVERY member builds their OWN version of ALL THREE modules, in their
own code roots. Nobody waits on anybody. The payoff at the end is that any
member's `watcher` can be repointed at another member's `converter` and
`persistence` by changing two configuration values and no code.

A solo reader does exactly the same and is simply the only member.

The tooling ("Dabbler") has a `docs/modules.yaml` manifest. Each module entry has:

- `slug` — machine identity, kebab-case, **must be unique within the manifest**
  (the product rejects a duplicate). Session sets stamp `module: <slug>` durably
  into their spec files, so a slug is expensive to change later.
- `title` — free text, what the Work Explorer tree actually renders, freely
  editable at any time.
- `codeRoots` — the paths the module owns; drives ownership routing (CODEOWNERS
  on GitHub, reviewer policies on Azure DevOps).

## Evidence already established, which you should treat as given

1. Nine modules render as **nine flat sibling rows**. Module grouping is exactly
   ONE level deep. There is no "member -> their three modules" sub-tree and none
   can be created.
2. Render order follows **manifest order**, not alphabetical. So authoring the
   manifest member-major keeps each person's three modules contiguous.
3. Nine declared modules with **zero** session sets render fine, no warnings.
4. All of the above was just re-confirmed against the running product (its own
   manifest parser, its own session-set discovery, its own renderer payload).

## The two candidate schemes

**Scheme A — version in the slug** (the pre-existing recommendation):
  slug `converter-v1`, title `Converter v1 - Priya`, code root `modules/priya/converter`

**Scheme B — owner in the slug**:
  slug `converter-priya`, title `Converter (Priya)`, code root `modules/priya/converter`

A known fact about Scheme A: it stays unique ONLY IF each member draws a
DISTINCT version number (Priya v1, Sam v2, Chen v3). If members do not
coordinate, and each naturally picks "v1", nine declarations collapse to three
slugs and the manifest rejects six of them. So Scheme A requires a central
version-number allocation step before anyone declares anything.

A known fact about Scheme B: it is unique with no allocation step, but a solo
reader's modules are named after themselves, and a member who leaves the team
leaves their name in durable slugs that sets have stamped.

## What to answer, as strict JSON and nothing else

{
  "recommended_scheme": "A" | "B" | "other",
  "slug_pattern": "<literal pattern, e.g. converter-priya>",
  "title_pattern": "<literal pattern>",
  "code_root_pattern": "<literal path pattern>",
  "manifest_order_rule": "<one sentence>",
  "codeowners_line_shape": "<a literal CODEOWNERS line, and the Azure DevOps equivalent>",
  "solo_reader_answer": "<what a solo reader with no teammates names their modules, concretely>",
  "member_leaves_answer": "<what happens to durable slugs when a member leaves>",
  "reasoning": "<the decisive argument, 3-6 sentences>",
  "strongest_objection_to_my_own_answer": "<the best case against what you just recommended>"
}

{
  "recommended_scheme": "B",
  "slug_pattern": "converter-priya",
  "title_pattern": "Priya - Converter",
  "code_root_pattern": "modules/priya/converter",
  "manifest_order_rule": "Declare modules in member-major order, keeping each member's converter, persistence, and watcher adjacent before listing the next member.",
  "codeowners_line_shape": "CODEOWNERS: /modules/priya/converter/ @priya ; Azure DevOps: required reviewer Priya with path filter /modules/priya/converter/*",
  "solo_reader_answer": "A solo reader named Alex should use `converter-alex`, `persistence-alex`, and `watcher-alex`, with code roots `modules/alex/converter`, `modules/alex/persistence`, and `modules/alex/watcher`.",
  "member_leaves_answer": "If Priya leaves, existing durable slugs such as `converter-priya` stay as-is in stamped session-set specs unless you intentionally run a migration; you may retitle or reassign ownership, but avoid slug renames.",
  "reasoning": "The more useful question is which slug axis is unique without coordination and unlikely to need renaming later. Version-in-slug fails that test because it requires a central allocation step up front and encodes a changing property, which directly violates the settled model that nobody waits on anybody. Owner-in-slug is unique at declaration time, aligns with the per-member code-root and reviewer-routing structure, and works cleanly with flat rendering when the manifest is authored member-major. Personal names in durable slugs are imperfect, but that drawback is smaller than the guaranteed collisions and coordination burden of version-based slugs.",
  "strongest_objection_to_my_own_answer": "Owner-based slugs hard-code a person into long-lived identifiers, so later handoff can leave awkward mismatches like `converter-priya` being maintained by someone else under a different path or title. A neutral, permanent instance ID would age better, but given the settled no-coordination model, the tooling does not offer an equally collision-free neutral axis."
}
